extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and informed readers of constitutional law, political science, and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria for evaluating the effectiveness, duties, and institutional quality of a national representative legislature (Congress) — focusing on its legislative, oversight, informational, organizational, and public-facing functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informing function preferred to legislative function
rubrics_metrics.description: The informing function of Congress should be preferred even to its legislative function; the assembly's duty to acquaint itself with and discuss administration is at least as important as making laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that Congress should 'inform' and 'guide' the people by discussing administration; 'The informing function of Congress should be preferred even to its legislative function.' Examples: debates and inquiries that enlighten the public are valuable; anti-pattern: focusing exclusively on passing many bills without illuminating administration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigilant oversight of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Vigilant oversight of administration is quite as important as legislation and must be exercised by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight means frequent, searching examination of administrative offices so that public confidence is secured and wrongdoing is detected. Anti-patterns: administrative 'isolation and privacy' that shield misconduct and prevent vindication of honesty; inadequate investigatory powers that make oversight ineffectual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for inquiry and searching investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative assembly should be inquisitive, enterprising, and irrepressible in its questioning — conducting cross-examinations and thorough inquiries into executive conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book praises Commons-style interrogation as 'the best conceivable source of information' and gives the example of Sir Robert Peel's experience of intense questioning. Guidance: equip members with means to ask and get answers; anti-pattern: limited or ceremonial questioning that fails to probe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and means to act on inquiry findings
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that the body which investigates also has the power to act effectively on the knowledge its inquiries secure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinct from the Press or public curiosity, Congress must not only uncover facts but have constitutional or practical means to translate findings into corrective action. Anti-pattern: inquiries that only inform but cannot change administration due to lack of authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherent leadership and policy direction
rubrics_metrics.description: A representative body ought not merely to echo public will but to lead it — to have recognized leadership, unity of purpose, and the capacity to drive the nation to conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective legislatures 'lead' and provide coherent policy direction; lacking 'recognized leaders' or organization results in wandering debates and disconnected measures. Anti-pattern: debates 'aimed at random' with no two measures 'consciously join[ing] in purpose.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate and scrutiny of administrative matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate of matters of administration is indispensable and often more important than debate of legislative problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing how execution and administration are carried out ('how the house is being built') matters more than knowing the original plans. Guidance: prioritize substantive discussion of administrative practice, oversight of implementation, and practical consequences over abstract legislative drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint and focus in legislative agenda (avoid overlegislation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should exercise restraint in lawmaking: avoid sending thousands of bills to committees and an omnivorous appetite for new subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes Congress for overdoing legislation, producing too many bills for even hasty thought. Guidance: concentrate on national interests, simplify and clarify legislative purposes by attention to administration. Anti-pattern: greedily taking up every possible subject and cluttering the legislative schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and openness of administration
rubrics_metrics.description: Administration should be open enough for quick and easy detection of fraud and for due vindication of honesty; Congress should provide the public with daily knowledge of important governmental transactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Openness increases public confidence in the executive; secrecy breeds suspicion and unjust doubts. Example: 'If the people could have...daily knowledge...their confidence in the executive...would...be very soon established.' Anti-pattern: privacies that 'cheat' honest administrators of reward and shield dishonesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability: aligning words with actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers and members should be accountable; there must be a 'day of reckoning' for words spoken so that policy utterances are matched by implementation and sponsorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes a system where 'nobody stands sponsor for the policy of the government' and where orators can speak without having to render account. Guidance: institutional mechanisms should bind rhetoric to responsibility; anti-pattern: talk without consequences—speeches forgotten before practice is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational capacity, recognized leadership, and adequate information
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislature needs recognized leaders, adequate information, and organizational structures from which definite policy can emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without leadership, information, or organization the House becomes 'meddlesome and inefficient.' Guidance: committees, leadership roles, reliable information channels, and internal organization are prerequisites for coherent policy-making; anti-patterns: factional, fickle chambers lacking guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper allocation of authority and avoidance of excessive multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive division and multiplication of authorities weakens strength, promptness, and wieldiness; powers should be allocated to avoid undue friction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that divided powers and many competing authorities cause 'unpleasant, wearing friction' and impede efficiency. Guidance: institutional design should seek suitable centralization or clearer allocation of responsibilities to ensure prompt and effective action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative efficiency, promptness, and unity of purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A national government must be strong, prompt, wieldy, and efficient; its strength lies in certainty and uniformity of purpose and unhesitating action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative institutions should enable administration that is steady, obedient to durable public judgments, and capable of clear execution. Anti-patterns: indistinct responsibility, roundabout processes, and lack of competent direction that produce inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional role in shaping public opinion versus press influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should inform and guide public opinion; a constitutional difficulty exists when the freedom and informational role of the Press exceeds that of Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author contrasts Congress (authority without informational freedom) with the Press (freedom without authority). Guidance: Congress must develop channels to inform the public so journalism does not become the de facto director of public understanding; anti-pattern: editors as 'self-constituted our guides' and caucuses deciding executive outcomes outside legislative accountability.
